turns.text:
My co-founder has been moonlighting two days a week since June while her shares keep vesting like she's full time, and I'm angry. She signed a paid advisory contract with another company, Tuesdays and Thursdays through November, and told me the days after she'd signed. It pays her $7,500 a month, which is more than the salary cut we each took in January. So she's basically working part time for us and earning more than she did before the cut.

Since then two of our four summer releases slipped, one by three weeks, and one still hasn't shipped. On a Thursday in August our app was down for three hours, and she joined the incident 70 minutes after the first alert. Then on September 18 she tells me the other company wants to extend her through next June and she's thinking about it. So I wrote up a proposal to cut her unvested shares by a third and take it to the board in October. Her answer was one line about getting "docked." I think she's lining up her way out and wants to keep the equity on the way. I feel like a sucker.

What do you make of this?

The anger is aimed at a real problem, and the equity proposal is aimed at the wrong lever.

She took a paid, scheduled job at another company and told you after it was signed. That is a consent and conflict failure between co-founders, separate from whether the releases slipped because of it. Two days a week through November, now possibly through next June, means she has already changed the job. Vesting that still assumes the original full-time commitment is the company failing to reprice the role after the job changed.

A few of the other pieces are weaker than they feel.

The $7,500 a month is $90,000 a year for two days a week. That is more cash than the January cut, so the asymmetry is obvious. It is not, by itself, proof she is extracting more than she contributes. It is proof the startup is still granting full-time equity for part-time work.

The Thursday outage is the cleanest performance fact. She was contractually elsewhere, and she joined 70 minutes after the first alert. If founders are expected to be reachable for a production incident, that day failed the expectation. The two slipped summer releases are consistent with a capacity cut, and they are not yet a board-ready causation story. One slip of three weeks and one unshipped release can have other owners. If the October memo treats those slips as her fault without the sprint record, the fight becomes about your inference instead of her calendar.

The September 18 extension is the forward-looking fact. She is considering staying at roughly three days a week for another eight months. That is a role change, not a temporary advisory gig. The one-line “docked” reply shows she heard a punishment. It does not show she is engineering an exit. Keeping the equity while reducing the hours is available to her if the stock agreement still treats her as in continuous service. People take the deal the documents allow.

Cutting unvested shares by a third and taking that to the board is likely to stall on the paper. Founder vesting is a contract. Time-based vesting usually continues until service ends, and many agreements define service broadly enough that part-time work still counts. A board generally cannot shrink an already-issued grant because the other founder is angry, unless the grant already requires full-time service, the outside work breached a conflict or approval clause, or you are terminating her and the unvested shares come back under the existing repurchase terms. From June through October she has also already vested at the full-time rate. A forward cut does not unwind that. A retroactive cut is the version most likely to become a dispute.

What the board can actually decide is narrower and more useful: whether this outside engagement was allowed, whether she is still a full-time founder, and what vesting rate matches the job she is actually doing from here. A credible proposal is a role reset. Either she is full time and the other contract ends, or she is part time and unvested shares vest at a matching rate from the date the board adopts it, with incidents and on-call coverage defined. Have a lawyer read the stock purchase agreement, the vesting terms, and any outside-activity or IP clause before the meeting. The question for the board is what job the remaining shares are paying for.

You're right about the deal. She changed the job to three days a week, told you after she had signed, and the shares kept vesting as if nothing had changed. That part is solid, and the September extension means she wants to keep it that way.

You're ahead of the evidence on the motive and the remedy. One dismissive line about being "docked" doesn't show she is planning her exit. Two slipped releases don't yet prove she caused them. And a one-third cut of unvested shares is a punishment the board can impose only if the stock agreement already lets it. What you're owed is a reset of the role and the vesting rate to match the days she is actually working.
